title: AI scams in Georgia and South Florida: How scammers use deepfakes to steal millions

reading.body:
Scammers are using AI deepfakes and voice cloning to impersonate real people, including an immigration attorney in South Florida. The technology creates convincing audio and visual content that allows criminals to target vulnerable populations, particularly immigrants seeking legal services. The deployment failure here is the absence of any verification system: potential victims receive calls and messages that appear to come from trusted professionals, but the criminals encounter no friction in impersonation.

What would have caught this is verification at the point of contact. When someone receives an urgent call claiming to be from an attorney or financial advisor, the system allows the caller to proceed without confirming their identity through an independent channel that the scammer cannot control. The victims had no way to verify they were speaking to the real person.

It is not established whether the AI systems used were purpose-built for fraud or repurposed from legitimate voice cloning and video generation tools.

summary:
Scammers are increasingly using artificial intelligence and deepfake technology to commit fraud across Georgia and South Florida. The FBI's 2025 Internet Crime Report found that Americans lost nearly $893 million to AI-enabled scams last year, with criminals using voice cloning, fake photos, and spoofed phone numbers to impersonate trusted individuals. In one case, a South Florida immigration attorney discovered criminals had cloned his voice to target immigrants, while a Cobb County couple lost approximately $800,000 in a cryptocurrency scam. Florida reported 350 AI-related complaints totaling nearly $40 million in losses, while Georgia had 71 complaints with over $10 million in losses.

Authorities say the technology is making familiar scams harder to detect by allowing criminals to create convincing emergency calls, romance schemes, and investment frauds. The FBI notes actual losses likely exceed reported figures since many victims don't report being scammed. To protect themselves, residents should establish code words with family members, verify urgent requests through known phone numbers, and avoid sending money based on unexpected calls. Banks recommend pausing before responding to requests for money or sensitive information and monitoring accounts closely.
